newsitem.title: USA: Kiwi will return to skies with limited capital.
newsitem.headline: Kiwi will return to skies with limited capital.

text.p: When Kiwi International Air Lines resumes operations on January 20, the low-cost airline will face the problems of limited capitalization and heightened regulatory scrutiny.
"They're starting way behind home plate. They will have a tough road ahead of them," said Steven Lewins, an airline analyst with Gruntal & Co.

Kiwi plans to resume scheduled service between Newark, N.J., Chicago, Atlanta and West Palm Beach, Fla., on January 20 using about half of its 15-plane fleet. The carrier plans to recall about 450 to 550 of the 1,200 workers who have been furloughed.
Kiwi will hold a press conference at 1300 EST/1800 GMT at the Newark Airport Marriott to provide details of its service plans.
The low-cost carrier declared bankruptcy in September and suspended operations in October. The airline was struggling under a $40 million debt load.

Kiwi received a $5 million investment commitment in December, but analysts fear the airline will continue to struggle without additional funding. Experts estimate the airline would need a cushion of about $3 million to $5 million for each aircraft to be successful.

Kiwi's efforts to build profitability during the first half of 1996 faltered after the May 11 crash of a ValuJet Inc airliner in the Florida Everglades. The accident, which killed 110 people, made consumers nervous about traveling with low-cost airlines.
Kiwi suffered another big setback in June when the U.S. Federal Aviation Administration ordered a partial shutdown of the airline to resolve record-keeping issues with a pilot-training program.

The U.S. Transportation Department last year touted the consumer benefits of low-cost airlines. The agency has since changed its tune and become more aggressive in monitoring upstarts. In December, the agency rejected ValuJet's plan to expand its service.
At the time of Kiwi's bankruptcy, many other new carriers were suffering from declining bookings. Load factors at regional airlines shrank In the wake of ValuJet crash.
In the quarter ended September 30, carriers such as Frontier Airlines Inc and Western Pacific Airlines Inc reported declining load factors and profits.

Vanguard Airlines Inc and AirWays Corp's AirTran airlines also suffered losses in the September quarter. JetTrain Corp, a Pennsylvania upstart, ceased operations in November after less than a year in service.
Still, Lewins said the "ValuJet factor" has been overblown as a reason for the poor performances by many of the upstarts.
"There is plenty of room for these little carriers to operate. But most of them don't survive," the analyst said.

The Airlines Pilots Association said that 94 percent of the start-ups that attempted to compete against major airlines between 1978 and 1992 failed. Since then, Reno Air Inc is the only start-up that has showed consistent profitability, the APA said in a report.
Reno Air remains one of the few to show improving load factors. The airline has been praised by analysts for carefully choosing markets and for controlling its growth.
